Other types are classified into groups covering pulmonary hypertension associated with cardiac, pulmonary, thromboembolic, or other disorders, for which management primarily involves treatment of the underlying disease. Pulmonary arterial hypertension3-8 is a progressive dis- ease with a high mortality rate, and patients appear to be prone to sudden death. Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hy- pertension occurs in patients of all ages and in both sexes but women in the fourth decade of life are those typically seen. A functional classification system similar to the New York Heart Association grades used for heart failure (see p.1165) may be used to indicate severity.1,2 Initial com- plaints include dyspnoea on exertion, fatigue, and chest discomfort or pain. In advanced disease, cor pulmonale (an enlargement of the right ventricle due to either dilata- tion, hypertrophy, or both) occurs and may progress to right-sided heart failure. The pulmonary arteries may also be affected by thromboembolic disease. The aim of treatment in pulmonary arterial hypertension has generally been to decrease the pulmonary arterial pres- sure, preferably in conjunction with an increase in cardiac output, and thus improve symptoms. However, more re- cent therapies also improve survival and reduce the need for transplantation, and this is reflected in current guidelines1,9,10 for management. Although most studies have been in patients with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, there is some evidence that patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with other dis- orders respond similarly,1,6,10 and they are usually man- aged in the same way. Improved understanding of the pathophysiology of pulmonary arterial hypertension has also led to the development of new treatments, although evidence of long-term benefit is limited in most cases. General treatment for pulmonary arterial hypertension1,9,10 includes measures to prevent hypoxia, since this causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, and treatment of associated right-sided heart failure. Oxygen therapy may be needed in some patients, and anaemia should be avoided. Pneumo- coccal and influenza vaccines are recommended to reduce the risk of pulmonary infections. Diuretics produce symp- tomatic benefit in patients with fluid retention, and should be given as appropriate. Digoxin has been used, although its role is less clearly established unless patients also have atrial fibrillation. Patients with pulmonary arterial hyper- tension also appear to be at risk of thromboembolic com- plications, and oral anticoagulation has been advised. Specific therapy has generally been based on the use of vasodilators.
